By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 16:03 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:05 EST, 23 November 2026.

Former Manchester United midfielder Paul Scholes has become the latest ex-Red Devil to tear into the club's defence, criticising Leny Yoro following his red card in his side's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off less than eight minutes into United's clash with their rivals at Anfield on Sunday, tripping Alexander Isak as he ran in on goal after an error from Matthijs de Ligt.

He has had a mixed time of things since his £52million move to Old Trafford in 2024, though has been playing in a leaky United defence that has conceded 23 goals in 11 Premier League matches this season – with only Crystal Palace conceding more.

Several different members of United's defence have come under fire this season, and, on Monday, it was the turn of Yoro.

'The Premier League at this minute just looks a little bit too much for him,' Scholes mentioned on The Good, The Bad and The Football, sponsored by Midnite.

Recent findings suggest that he added: 'You know what, he’s come in to a really bad setup defensively now. I think they also made the point yesterday if he went in next to (Virgil) Van Dijk he might look a little bit better but he doesn’t look Premier League level. He looks like a rabbit in the headlights.'.

Paul Scholes (pictured) has suggested Leny Yoro is not yet ready for the Premier League.

Yoro was sent off in the opening minutes of Manchester United's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool.

Sources indicate that fellow former United midfielder Nicky Butt, who played alongside Scholes for United between 1994 and 2004, added: 'If that’s Man United in our day, he’s on loan like a Jonny Evans or a John O’Shea. He’s a great talent that will come good.'.

Scholes, though, wasn't having any of it.

He replied: 'I’m not sure how much of a great talent he is. I think he has shown a little bit of a sign in the France squad but every time I’ve seen him he doesn’t look at the races. Everything’s happening around him and he’s just a bit, oh, what do I do?'.

United have also faced criticism for their apparent lack of running this season, with eyebrows raised when Youri Tielemans remarked in the summer that they didn't do much prior to the campaign getting under way.

Sources indicate that the club rank 17th for distance covered in the top flight this season, with Liverpool, Brentford and Everton below them. The latter two will almost certainly pass them though after their game on Monday.

That, according to Butt, is down to the players.

'We’ve had our say about the players and they’re just not good enough,' he stated. 'It is the most unathletic team I’ve ever seen in Man United.

'I’m going to go through a team and I’m trying to be as honest as I can. Forget the quality for right now. For me, physicality-wise, if you go through a team, the right back, he’s physically OK, but he’s not amazing. De Ligt or Harry, whoever he’s going to play in there, physically not great. Martinez for me is physically not great. You got Yoro who will physically come good.

Nicky Butt (pictured), meanwhile, has criticised the physical ability of many of United's players.

Sources indicate that 'Then I go on to the midfield, none of them are physically good enough. Kobbie can get about the pitch 15-20 yards, but he’s not box to box. Stated that numerous times. He’s got a lot of talent. He’s got a lot of things going for him. I think he’s a top player. He ain’t got the legs. He needs to have legs around him but his legs around him at the minute are Bruno and Tielemans - and they can’t run around.

In a recent development, 'Look at Mbeumo, I think he’s OK but he’s not going to blow anybody away. I think Cunha can run. So then you look at the whole squad and you’re saying three players can run.

'What I’m getting at there, and it sounds like I’m being a draconian but what you have to do first and foremost when you go to Anfield is to be able to compete physically and they can’t so they have no chance.'.

By Freddie Cotton | 24 Nov 2026 20:48, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 20:58.

Marseille welcome Levski Sofia to the Stade Velodrome on Thursday evening on matchday five of the 2026-27 UEFA Europa League campaign.

In their previous competition outing, Les Olympiens claimed a crucial 1-0 win away to Bayer Leverkusen, while the Blues beat Polish side Jagiellonia by the same scoreline at the National Stadium Vasil Levski.

After narrowly missing out on booking their place in the UEFA Champions League for the second consecutive year last season, finishing fifth in Ligue 1 and just one point below Lyon in fourth, Marseille will be extremely disappointed with how they have performed on the continent so far this campaign.

Although they edged out Leverkusen in their latest Europa League fixture, losses to Sturm Graz, Olympiacos and Besiktas in each of their opening three matches mean Bruno Genesio’s men have earned just three points so far in Europe, leaving them 31st in the league phase table and outside of the knockout stage places.

Despite conceding two late goals to lose against Le Mans on Sunday evening, Les Olympiens have seen a huge improvement in their league endeavours, having won each of their prior five matches to right now sit fifth in the Ligue 1 table and just three points outside the automatic Champions League qualification places.

Marseille are yet to claim victory over Levski, though they do boast a mainly positive record against Bulgarian opposition, having beaten CSKA Sofia in each of their other two meetings with efbet League sides.

Having won their first efbet League title since 2009 last season and finished 10 points ahead of runners-up Ludogorets, who had triumphed in each of the previous 14 consecutive campaigns, Levski competed in the qualifying stages of the Champions League for the first time in 17 years during the summer.

The Blues impressed in their efforts for tournament qualification, beating Borac Banja Luka, Univ Craiova and Kairat Almaty to progress to the decisive playoff tie, but having endured a 4-0 aggregate defeat against Greek giants AEK Athens, the Bulgarian side are instead competing in the Europa League this season.

However, Julio Velazquez’s men have given a good account of themselves so far on the continent as after taking just one point from their first two matches, Levski have won back-to-back matches in the Europa League to sit 10th in the standings with seven points and only outside the round-of-16 positions on goal difference.

While the Blues do not have the best recent record against French opposition, having won just one of their previous four meetings with Ligue 1 sides, that triumph did come over Marseille, with Levski securing a 1-0 win over Les Olympiens in the group stages of this competition in December 2005, when it was branded as the UEFA Cup.

On a more positive note, after missing the match against Leverkusen as a precaution, Moroccan forward Amine Harit has started Les Olympiens’ previous two league fixtures and looks set to return to feature from the off in the week too.

Netting eight Ligue 1 goals so far this season, including one in each of his previous four outings, Algerian forward Amine Gouiri is undoubtedly the hosts’ biggest threat going forward and will be hoping to add to his winner against Leverkusen last time out in the competition.

Having been left out of Levski’s Europa League squad list, Oliver Kamdem, Mustapha Sangare and Petko Hristov are all unavailable for Thursday’s fixture, while 34-year-old striker Radoslav Kirilov remains out with a knee problem.

Recent findings suggest that however, the Blues will be delighted to have welcomed midfielder Asen Mitkov back from injury against Lok. Sofia on Sunday afternoon and the 21-year-old will be hopeful for more minutes in the week too.

Contributing to six goals in 12 league appearances, Portuguese midfielder Serginho has been the visitors’ dangerman so far this season and will be hoping to replicate his efbet League form on the continent this week.

Having finally bounced back from their three-game losing streak in the Europa League by claiming an important win over Leverkusen in their latest European outing, Marseille will certainly be aiming to fight their way into the knockout progression places with victory on Thursday evening.

While Levski have made a promising start to their campaign, we think Les Olympiens will bag all three points at the Stade Velodrome this week and are backing them to mount a late charge for a top-eight finish in the league phase.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

Sources indicate that in this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are at the moment level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

In a recent development, he stated: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”.

Recent findings suggest that what a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Sources indicate that just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”.

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

Last week Viking marked their home debut in the Champions League by securing a famous 3-3 draw with heavyweights Bayern Munich. They had led 2-0 at half-time before rescuing a point in the last minute.

Hopes of another famous European night here never appeared likely, even though their 2,500 travelling supporters remained noisy all evening.

Villa were awarded a second goal after Alysson was brought down in the penalty area by Zlatko Tripic.

The spot kick was awarded more than a minute after the actual incident following a recommendation from VAR, with Austrian referee Sebastian Gishamer watching it again on the TV monitor. Emiliano Buendía calmly dispatched the penalty to put Villa in total control.

Yet Alysson had proved a threat on the right flank all evening and in the 62nd minute proved pivotal in the third goal.Running on to Buendía’s pass from the halfway line, Alysson advanced into the area and his shot took a big deflection off Henrik Heggheim to beat Ostbo at the near post.

Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that getting playing time is key to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country .
  • Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception.
  • It has been revealed that but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that getting playing time is key to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Sources indicate that unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

It has been revealed that but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

In a recent development, "I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can.".

It has been revealed that A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment.".

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

Como beat Cagliari 2-0 with two headers from Yan Couto crosses, moving back into fourth place on 26 points. Juventus visit next and trail the side holding the last Champions League place by eight points.

In a recent development, como beat Cagliari 2-0 at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia on Saturday, 21 November 2026. Both goals were headers, and Yan Couto crossed for both of them. The result lifted Fàbregas’ side back into fourth place. That is the last Champions League place, and Juventus are the next visitors.

Ramón opened the scoring after 24 minutes. He met Couto’s cross from the right and headed past goalkeeper Caprile. Da Cunha, the captain, doubled the lead in the 56th minute. He headed in another Couto delivery from the centre of the area.

Fàbregas left Nico Paz and Perrone on the bench. The two Argentinians had rejoined the squad only hours before kick-off after international duty. Como play AEK in the Champions League on Tuesday. Even without the pair from the start, the hosts kept Cagliari out. Both men entered in the 57th minute, with Liberali and Milla making way respectively. It was Como’s first win since a defeat to Inter before the international break.

It has been revealed that for Fàbregas, the performance was not perfect, but he was very pleased. Perrone had a minor problem, the coach explained, which ruled out a full 90 minutes for the midfielder.

According to recent reports, como have now won three Serie A home games in a row without conceding, which they last did in October and November 1984, according to Sportmediaset. Da Cunha has three goals in his last four games across Serie A and the Champions League. Fàbregas has never lost to Cagliari in five Serie A matches as a coach. He has won three of them and drawn two. Cagliari have lost each of their last four away league games. That is their first run of four straight away defeats in Serie A since November–December 2023.

Industry observers note that in that table, Juventus’ record reads five wins, three draws and three defeats. They have scored 15 goals and conceded 12. The gap to Como stood at eight points before Juventus’ game against Venezia.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matt Law | 24 Nov 2026 21:10, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 21:12.
  • Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has refused to confirm whether Luke Shaw will be involved in Wednesday's Champions League clash with Sporting Lisbon.
  • Shaw has made the trip to Portugal alongside his teammates, having recovered from the muscular problem that has sidelined him since the early stages of October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 24 Nov 2026 21:10, Last updated: 24 Nov 2026 21:12.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has refused to confirm whether Luke Shaw will be involved in Wednesday's Champions League clash with Sporting Lisbon.

Shaw has made the trip to Portugal alongside his teammates, having recovered from the muscular problem that has sidelined him since the early stages of October.

The 31-year-old has been a huge miss at the back for Man United, and Pochettino has welcomed the Englishman's return to fitness.

However, it remains to be seen whether he is involved against Sporting.

“All the players need to feel they can have an impact for the team and they can perform," Pochettino told reporters during his pre-game press conference.

“It’s up to us to give the opportunities to every single player in the moment that we believe that they deserve to be involved in the game.

“Of course, I know Luke from the past, in our time in Southampton, but all [of us who are] involved, we are not the same people now. It’s more than 10 years ago.

“Obviously, it’s good to see him and he came from a small issue but now he needs to recover his best form.

“It’s good to have him, because he’s experienced everything with the squad, but we’ll see if he can be involved tomorrow or not, from the beginning or during the game.”.

Matheus Cunha is suspended for the match following his red card against Roma in the team's last European fixture, while Benjamin Sesko, Marcus Rashford, Carlos Baleba and Manuel Ugarte are all injured for the 20-time English champions.

Pochettino also insisted during his press conference that Man United are 'not a fragile team' despite their huge difficulties this season.

The Red Devils will enter the game with Sporting off the back of a 4-0 defeat to Liverpool, and they currently sit down in 19th spot in the Premier League table.

Recent findings suggest that "We are not fragile, we are a strong team who last season finished third. Sometimes things happen in football for different reasons. We need to identify why and we are working on it. I think we are going to turn the situation around," remarked the head coach.

#186180. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious.
  • But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.
  • Sources indicate that this is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men.".

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

Sources indicate that this is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," states Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

Sources indicate that the exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In a recent development, in the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing fresh or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people.".

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski notes the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," claims Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued.".

In a recent development, on October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The problem of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

In a recent development, since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

In a recent development, martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

In a recent development, germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

Recent findings suggest that "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi mentioned. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

Dundee boss Steven Pressley states he felt hurt and embarrassed after losing 8-0 to Hearts.

‘It’s hard to put your finger on one certain thing. Maybe just being more decisive in both boxes or probably conceding goals at crucial times in the game, like after five minutes on Saturday, we just give ourselves a bit of a mountain to climb.’.

It looked like Marink Reedijk’s side had turned the corner when they followed up a rousing victory over city rivals Hearts in the Premier Sports Cup semi-final with a 4-0 win at Aberdeen in their last game before the international break.

Sources indicate that so McGrath is hoping Saturday’s aberration was a blip. ‘We’ve been on a decent run the last month and probably the international break came at a tricky time for us. Vincenzo Montella’s time with AC Milan was ‘a dream’ for him, but he failed to achieve much during his time at the helm.

Looking back on Montella’s time leading Milan is tricky. On paper, the Italian had a strong tenure at the club, achieving a 50% win rate and only losing 18 of his 64 games in charge at San Siro, not a terrible record by any means.

He even ended a five-year trophy drought with a win against Juventus in the Supercoppa Italiana and returned the Rossoneri to Europe, with a sixth-place finish in the 2016/17 season. In itself, that was a first since 2014.

It has been revealed that this is where context matters, though. The start of the 2017/18 season was tough, as the Diavolo won six of their first 14 games and he was sacked before December. Despite that, he still views the club in an excellent light.

Speaking to La Gazzetta dello Sport’s ‘La Tripletta’ podcast, Montella went over his time with the club and how he fulfilled a dream by taking the job, as MilanPress relays.

“It was a fantastic experience there [at Milan] too, it was my dream. Then, as a professional, it’s a little different, but when I was thirteen I was a fan of that AC Milan team. My older brother took me to see Maradona’s Napoli team twice to make me a Napoli fan, and Maradona scored three goals.

It has been revealed that “Despite this, my idol was Van Basten because I was a striker: I studied him and dreamed of becoming like him, and so I was a Milan fan. I knew everything about Milan, so for me it was an incredible feeling to join Milan.”.

According to recent reports, “He liked to talk about football; he liked to give advice even when it was a bit out of context at the time, because he always had the mentality of having Van Basten as a centre forward with Papin, a two-time Ballon d’Or winner, on the bench. He wanted me to play with two strikers, and I tried to plug the gap for months.

In a recent development, “I told him it was difficult; I knew all the lineups of those years. I was a Milan fan: the starter was Van Basten and the reserve was Papin, both Ballon d’Or winners. So, ‘If you buy me some players like that, rest assured that I’ll play them both.'”.

“It was a year when we returned to Europe. I think it had been two or three years since Milan had been there, and it was something new at the time. We won a trophy, a small one. Just the other night I saw Galliani at a dinner; he reminded me of it and remembers it perfectly.

“I have to say that I found him to be the perfect manager at the time, because he was always on my side when it came to pressure; he gave me complete autonomy in my decisions and he helped me with everything, from the number of collaborators to new things; whatever I asked for, he was always on the coach’s side.

“And so for me he was truly an incredible manager, who in that phase, in that change, was fundamental even in achieving these small results, especially after Berlusconi’s great AC Milan.

Sources indicate that “We deserved to win even in regulation time: we had some easy chances to win it, then it came to penalties. Gigio saved the penalty from Dybala, who kicked it really hard, but he filled the net with it.”.

“I was a little worried from the beginning because there was this obsession with publicising everything, almost like a publicity stunt, so I was a little worried. In theory, there was sharing, at least that’s what it looked like, but I couldn’t back out when in reality that wasn’t always the case.

“And so sometimes there were players I hadn’t even consulted about, who would arrive and then say, ‘It was shared,’ and when you’re there, you can’t say otherwise. Certainly, when you build a team and have the budget, the first thing you do is: we had a goalkeeper, I’ll get a centre forward, we were missing a centre forward.

Industry observers note that “In the final selection, the centre forward was the only one left, with a budget of 15-20 million. And then Kalinic… yes, I chose him because that was the final budget. So our, let’s say, second-choice striker was paid thirty-eight million, if I remember correctly, who was André Silva, and the first striker was paid half that.

“And so, in my opinion, a misunderstanding of this kind was created, with so many changes, even though at that stage we weren’t even playing badly for having fifteen new players.

“We still had Calhanoglu, who wasn’t feeling well, coming off months of suspension. The team was still being built: we weren’t in line with the Scudetto objectives that had been announced, but certainly, given our development, we were absolutely on target.

“Who would I have signed up front? At the time, we were probably negotiating for Aubameyang, if I remember correctly. Ronaldo? No, I didn’t believe it, not at all.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.

It has been revealed that people entering their golden years now have better memory and experience slower cognitive decline than previous generations. A study of people born between 1910 and 1964 found that a ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Researchers speculate that improvements in memory might be thanks to better education, health care and nutrition in childhood, while the slower decline in cognitive function might be influenced by factors later in life, such as improved treatment for cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

Reference: Nature Medicine paper.

In a recent development, the large language models that underlie chatbots such as ChatGPT are rapidly overcoming some of their weaknesses, say computer scientists Owen Queen and James Zou. They analysed flaws — such as hallucinating references — that had been flagged by researchers in academic papers. Most flaws were no longer a problem within roughly 16 months of a paper’s publication — for example, the latest models hardly ever attribute information to sources that don’t exist. On the other hand, newer models are getting more sycophantic and worse at generating random numbers.

Reference: Owen Queen & James Zou blog post.

Undergraduate students were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging variants of the SARS-CoV-2 virus between 2021 and 2023, according to a massive genetic analysis. Researchers found that viral transmission during that period was highest among school students between the ages of 15 and 18, university undergrads and nursing-home residents. However, staff at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. The study’s scale “is truly impressive”, indicates infectious-disease researcher Bill Hanage.

A report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) suggests that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, and standards for doing so are applied inconsistently across journals. NASEM recommends that the editorial review process be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months. The report was due to be published on 19 November, but was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained references with fabricated author names, which could suggest that artificial intelligence was used to draft or edit it.

Industry observers note that earlier this week we tried our hands at a game that tests our ability to decode ‘tortured phrases’ — ridiculous synonyms for common terms, which are intended to obscure plagiarism. For example, instead of ‘substantial data’, a study might use ‘colossal information’. The quiz inspired Briefing reader Chris Schneider to suggest her own tongue-in-cheek tortured phrase for our own dear ‘Nature Briefing’: “Essence of donning underwear.”.

In a recent development, in the spirit of silliness, we’d like to hear your best science-related tortured phrases — whether spotted in the wild or invented just for fun. Entertain us at briefing@nature.com.

Recent findings suggest that bees are the well-deserved superstars of the pollination world, and the reputations of birds, bats and even wasps are on the rise. Make room, now, for flies. Diptera — especially hoverflies (Syrphidae) — are undervalued pollinators. For example, on strawberry farms in England, hoverflies can make up more than half of the pollinating insects. Meanwhile, our reliance on managed honeybees can actually damage biodiversity and crop quality.

The New Yorker | 16 min read (intermittent paywall).

An artificially intelligent human wants to make choices that matter in The right to do wrong.

In a recent development, for the first time, astrophysicists have directly observed a giant star — one that’s swelling in size toward the end of its life cycle — engulfing a nearby ‘companion’ star in its gas envelope. Now they wait to learn what comes next. The companion star could cause the giant star to shed its gas envelope, after which the two could settle into a tight orbit; or it could plunge into the giant star’s core to its doom. “To conclusively rule out either case, we need to continue observing the system,” claims astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar.

Space physicist Emma Bunce has been working on the European–Japanese BepiColombo mission for 20 years. After an eight-year journey battling the Sun's immense gravitational pull, if all goes well, it will finally enter Mercury’s orbit tomorrow. (The Guardian | 3 min read).

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03816-3.

By Joel Lefevre | 24 Nov 2026 23:33.

In a matchup featuring two of Ligue 1's biggest surprise stories at the moment, Brest will welcome Paris FC to Stade Francis-Le Ble on Friday.

A 1-0 win at Strasbourg on matchday 11 lifted the Brittany side to sixth in the Ligue 1 table, five points behind Paris, who are second after a convincing 4-0 triumph over Angers.

It appears as though Julien Lachuer has finally figured out the right buttons to push to help Brest find some consistency domestically.

This team entered November having dropped points in four of their last five league fixtures, but they will boast a 100% record this month should they triumph on Friday.

Brest can also win at least four domestic affairs in a row for the first time in a single league season since 2023-24 when they claimed six consecutive victories in this competition.

With a win on matchday 12, they would temporarily move into third place in Ligue 1 and that final Champions League spot above Lille on goal difference.

A team that gave up at least one goal in each of their first eight matches in this competition have not conceded in their last three such games.

After 11 matchdays, Les Pirates are third in Ligue 1 regarding expected goals but also rank third in significant chances missed (23).

Liam Rosenior must be happy to be back in France, managing in a league where he has found tremendous success as a head coach.

The man who guided Strasbourg to a place in the Conference League has transformed Paris FC into title contenders, with his side just three points below Paris Saint-Germain heading into this match.

A victory by three or more goals on Friday would temporarily put them in first place and extend their winning run in this competition to four matches.

Right now, Paris FC are averaging 2.09 points per match in this competition, which is 0.80 more than a season ago, the biggest such increase among Ligue 1 clubs over that span.

They boast the lowest expected goals conceded in the league (10.2) and are one of three teams in the top flight that have not allowed a set-piece goal so far, with PSG and Lens being the others.

Paris FC can earn a third successive Ligue 1 triumph versus Brest on Friday, beating them 2-1 in their last visit to Stade Francis-Le Ble a season ago.

A calf strain may keep Brendan Chardonnet out of the Brest fold on Friday, while Kenny Lala is questionable with a knock and Kamory Doumbia is also doubtful with an ankle injury.

Noah Edjouma netted his third of the competition last week, while Egil Selvik stopped five shots to collect his third successive clean sheet in Ligue 1.

Meanwhile, for Paris FC, Nhoa Sangui may miss another match because of a hamstring concern which he has struggled to recover from.

Patrick Zabi, Luca Koleosho, Maxime Lopez and Diego Coppola all found the back of the net on matchday 11, with each strike coming in the second half.

Brest possible starting lineup:.

Selvik; Zogbe, Tousart, Lloris, Locko; Chotard, Magnetti; Edjouma, Nonge, Mboup; Ajorque.

Paris FC possible starting lineup:.

Trapp; Matondo, Chergui, Coppola, Otavio; Lopez, Lees-Melou; Kebbal, Zabi, Pagis; Koleosho.

While Brest are trending in the right direction, Paris FC have shown more consistency all season, and we believe their overall balance will see them collect maximum points once again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z.

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

Recent findings suggest that and that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”.

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Recent findings suggest that kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

In a recent development, it has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

According to recent reports, kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Industry observers note that vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Sources indicate that arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.
  • In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.
  • Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," noted Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," noted Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy.".

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

In a recent development, "We are seeing a striking contrast," noted Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum.".

Sources indicate that that momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," remarked CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

Recent findings suggest that the G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low.".

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

It has been revealed that however, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, noted the report.

The authors stated these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action.".

In a recent development, frosinone looked to commit numbers into Milan’s half, creating ball-sided overloads to progress through the pitch. Their two wingers maintained wide positions to stretch Milan’s wing-backs and create more space in the central areas.

Industry observers note that out of possession, Frosinone adopted a 3-4-3 to match Milan’s 3-4-2-1 in possession. They also maintained a very high defensive line, looking to press Milan aggressively and win the ball back as high up the pitch as possible.

Milan allowed Frosinone to dictate possession, dropping into a deeper defensive block to invite them into their half. Once Frosinone advanced, Milan looked to win the ball back and launch quick counter-attacks.

Industry observers note that frosinone’s lack of a clear attacking structure and, more importantly, an organised rest defence left them vulnerable in transition. Milan exploited this disorganisation repeatedly, with the next four goals all benefiting from the spaces Frosinone left behind.

By Ben Sully | 25 Nov 2026 00:26, Last updated: 25 Nov 2026 00:26.

Brentford are reportedly among three Premier League clubs interested in signing Lazio midfielder Kenneth Taylor.

The Bees splashed out around £41m to recruit midfielder Mamadou Sangare from Lens in the summer in a club-record transfer.

Sangare has featured in all 11 of Brentford's Premier League games, but he has not always been a guaranteed starter due to the competition from Vitaly Janelt and Yehor Yarmoliuk.

Mathias Jensen is also available to Brentford boss Keith Andrews, who currently has plenty of options at his disposal in central midfield.

However, Jensen is out of contract at the end of the season, and the uncertainty surrounding his future may be one of the factors behind Brentford's apparent interest in Taylor.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the Bees are one of three Premier League clubs that are keeping tabs on the Dutchman's performances at Lazio.

Bournemouth and Newcastle United are also showing a keen interest as they scour the market for potential midfield recruits.

The Cherries are believed to view Taylor as a potential replacement for Alex Scott, who continues to draw interest from some of the Premier League's biggest clubs.

Meanwhile, Newcastle appear to be still open to bolstering a midfield that lost the services of Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali at the end of last season, despite recruiting Nico Gonzalez and Aladji Bamba in the summer window.

Taylor has played regularly since joining Lazio from Ajax in January, contributing five goals and five assists in 34 competitive appearances.

In fact, he has registered two goals and three assists in 12 league matches this term, helping Gennaro Gattuso's side establish a two-point lead at the top of Serie A.

With Taylor under contract until June 2030, there is a belief his potential suitors will have to offer around €40m (£33m) to have any hope of prising him away from Lazio.

However, a January departure seems unlikely at this stage, with Gattuso keen to keep one of his key players for the club's title battle.

Brentford, Bournemouth and Newcastle will also have to be aware of rival interest from Juventus, who view him as the 'ideal' midfield target.

#186164. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's crucial.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's crucial.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black?
  • Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
  • Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

It has been revealed that but to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a upcoming task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

Sources indicate that there's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?".

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

According to recent reports, and the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Recent findings suggest that maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great upcoming idea.

According to recent reports, but it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

It has been revealed that scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Industry observers note that protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

In a recent development, take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

In a recent development, try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

Industry observers note that you can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

Aberdeen boss Mario Frick's heavy metal football is music to the ears of their long-suffering supporters

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.
  • Published: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026.
  • As they embarked on the long journey home from Kilmarnock on Saturday night, Aberdeen supporters would surely have felt a little extra spring in their step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026.

As they embarked on the long journey home from Kilmarnock on Saturday night, Aberdeen supporters would surely have felt a little extra spring in their step.

If 2026 felt like it had been shaping up to be something of an annus horribilis, a 4-2 victory at Rugby Park undoubtedly lifted some of the gloom that had been hanging over the club these past few months.

In a recent development, granted, a sample size of only one match under Mario Frick is very small. Nobody would be of a mind to get carried away with themselves just yet, especially given that Killie are easily the worst team in the league.

But there was enough in the performance, particularly during a first half which saw them score three goals in 30 minutes, to suggest that a brighter future could lie ahead under the newly introduced manager.

According to recent reports, aberdeen were aggressive, they played on the front foot, and they attacked with pace. Most of all, they were actually exciting and entertaining to watch.

It has been revealed that those were boxes they never ticked at any point during Stephen Robinson's time in charge. Robinson failed at Aberdeen and his team were routinely awful in terms of the quality of football they served up.

Mario Frick celebrates after a 4-2 win over Kilmarnock in his first game as Aberdeen manager.

Ante Palaversa is back in the Aberdeen team after becoming the forgotten man of Pittodrie.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet rediscovered the feelgood factor by scoring twice at Rugby Park.

In the space of only 90 minutes, Frick did more to send a wave of positivity through supporters than Robinson ever managed to do in his eight months at the helm.

The shift in mood has been as profound as it has been instantaneous, with Frick's so-called heavy metal football music to the fans' ears.

Headlines of Super Mario were always likely to follow, but Frick and his players will face an altogether tougher examination when they take on Rangers at Ibrox tomorrow.

It is an intriguing contest on various levels, with Rangers unbeaten in 13 matches as Derek McInnes goes up against his former club once again.

Given that these teams met in the Premier Sports Cup only a few weeks ago, perhaps the greatest barometer of Frick's impact will be whether Aberdeen can pose more of a threat than they did at Hampden.

But what has changed? After such a turgid run of form that left players looking completely bereft of any confidence and cohesion, how was Frick able to generate an immediate improvement?

Speaking after the win at Killie, Frick was asked what sort of message he had given to the players given that time together on the training pitch had been fairly limited.

According to recent reports, 'I told them they should play like they did when they were young. In those days they didn't think about mistakes.

'They didn't think about anything negative. They played only to win, for fun.'.

It was simple but refreshing. In an age of increasingly complex coaching jargon, Frick's message was intended to liberate his players – and it worked a treat.

Recent findings suggest that aberdeen went 2-0 up inside 12 minutes, with Kevin Nisbet scoring twice. The team looked free from the trauma of the Robinson era.

Even when Kilmarnock fought back and the game became more chaotic, Aberdeen retained enough attacking threat and collective belief to close it out.

Industry observers note that it was a huge result. A defeat would have dropped Aberdeen to the foot of the table. Instead, they climbed five places and, more importantly, rediscovered a feelgood factor.

In his previous utterances, Frick was clear that goalscoring has been the central problem.

It has been revealed that his previous teams at Vaduz and Luzern were known for their attacking output. At Luzern last season they scored 76 goals.

According to recent reports, aberdeen had managed only 12 in 12 league matches before his arrival. The early evidence suggests the players have absorbed the message quickly.

Frick's insistence on the basics – aggression, willingness to work, positive body language – appears to have cut through more effectively than more elaborate instructions might have done.

According to recent reports, this is consistent with the picture painted by those who worked with him in Switzerland. Frick is not a rigid systems coach wedded to a single formation.

According to recent reports, he has most often used a 4-4-2 diamond, but the shape is secondary to the mentality. High pressing to force turnovers, rapid counter-attacks, and a sense of freedom imbued to his players.

According to recent reports, all of which makes tomorrow's clash at Ibrox all the more compelling. Aberdeen have lost their last eight meetings with Rangers in all competitions.

The previous two encounters this season, one in the Premiership and one in the Premier Sports Cup, were both settled by late Rangers goals.

The contrast in styles will be stark. Rangers are likely to control territory and force Aberdeen to defend for longer periods than they did at Rugby Park.

Frick's side will need to show that the freedom he has granted them does not dissolve into naivety when the opponent is stronger and more experienced.

The high press that worked so effectively against a struggling Killie side will have to be timed with greater precision.

According to recent reports, the attacking play will require clinical decision-making in the final third. And the defensive structure, which Frick identified as the main area for improvement after Saturday, will be examined under more sustained pressure.

Frick has already spoken of aiming higher than mere survival. In a league which is always extremely tight in the mid-table, top six should be the minimum target.

It has been revealed that that may have sounded optimistic a fortnight ago. But the win at Kilmarnock suggested Aberdeen have enough about themselves to be looking up rather than over their shoulders.

The squad still needs greater consistency and, in certain areas, greater quality.

But there is already evidence to suggest he can get a tune out of some players who either under-performed under Robinson or, in some cases, those who had been totally discarded.

Ante Palaversa would surely be chief among them. The Croatian midfielder hardly kicked a ball under Robinson and had become the forgotten man at Pittodrie.

Brought in to make his first league start of the season, his performance at Killie and the way he controlled things in midfield made his exclusion under Robinson look all the more bizarre.

None of this is to say that Aberdeen are suddenly a top-class football team. At best, they remain very much a work in progress.

Yet, crucially, Frick immediately has the supporters onboard in a way that Robinson never managed to do.

Frick and his players could yet be given a major reality check if they were to suffer a hefty defeat to a Rangers side unbeaten in 13 matches.

But there is belief and positivity in the camp at Pittodrie. Feelgood factors in football can often be fragile and often short-lived, but they are also real.

When players begin to play with freedom and confidence, results usually tend to take care of themselves.

Frick has not yet transformed Aberdeen. He has, however, given the players and the fans a reason to believe that a brighter future could lie ahead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Tarkowski picked up the first red of his Premier League career on Monday night and let’s be honest, we all thought he had more than that.
  • Tarkowski was shown the red for the follow-through on a tackle on Brentford’s Yehor Yarmolyuk which saw his name crossed off a list of players who have surprisingly never received a red.
  • A career of 323 games and not a single red card is an impressive feat from King.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Tarkowski picked up the first red of his Premier League career on Monday night and let’s be honest, we all thought he had more than that.

Tarkowski was shown the red for the follow-through on a tackle on Brentford’s Yehor Yarmolyuk which saw his name crossed off a list of players who have surprisingly never received a red.

Here are the remaining candidates:.

A career of 323 games and not a single red card is an impressive feat from King.

The former Tottenham defender’s struggles with injuries are well known with him only twice playing more than 30 Premier League games in a single season but when he was on the pitch, he was as composed as can be.

Not only did King never get his marching orders, he only got nine yellows in every match he played.

King’s numbers are impressive, but the record belongs to Hughes.

The former Newcastle, Fulham and Aston Villa man played 455 Premier League matches but never received a red card.

In total, the Northern Irishman played 675 games in his career and was never sent off, earning 19 yellows in that time.

Considering how composed he often looked, perhaps we could not be too surprised that Lahm features on this list.

He played in eight different positions in his career but never once was so out of his depth that he got himself sent off.

Lahm primarily operated as a full-back with 269 appearances on the right and 219 on the left before Pep Guardiola converted him into a defensive midfielder.

He did quite like a yellow though, getting 49 in his career.

Considering he played the majority of his career as a sweeper, it is particularly impressive that Italian legend Scirea was never sent off.

The World Cup and European Cup-winning defender played 621 times and yet was never given his marching orders.

To make it even more impressive, in his long career, which featured 551 games for Juventus, Scirea got just four yellow cards.

The former Match of the Day host is well known for having not only never received a red, but never even got booked either.

Lineker played 468 games, the majority of which were in the First Division, and yes he was a striker but we could show you a long list of number nines who have picked up a red.

The closest Lineker ever came was in Euro 1992 when he stamped on Basile Boli’s toe. The ref missed it and the pre-VAR world meant Lineker was in the clear.

Not only did Barnes never receive a red, but he was also the first player to make it past 100 Premier League games without a card of either colour.

Barnes played most of his football pre-Premier League, getting 349 appearances in the old First Division before making 201 in the Premier League, but never got a red.

He ended his career with 696 games played and not a single entry in the referee’s book.

Sources indicate that iniesta getting a red card just feels wrong, doesn’t it? Well, the good news is it’s never happened.

Iniesta played 885 games in his career, 674 of which were for Barcelona, but never received a red card.

He did pick up a fair few yellows, having got 74 in his time.

Considering he was quite a robust winger, Duff being on this list is surprising.

He played 629 games, starting off with Blackburn before moving to Chelsea in 2003, yet never got a red card.

Instead, he got 42 yellows, the majority of which came with Rovers, but he was largely a clean player.
